To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
upward mobility is a process that is not only experienced but also perceived and that it can be a cause of both anxiety and pleasure.

the Changers have experienced upward mobility, and that the men have qualitatively attempted to appear ‘middleclass’ by consuming expensive commodities and by replicating the didactic, ‘posh’ masculinity which is produced via sections of the mass media.
upward mobility is a complex, contradictory and anxiety-inducing process that can be understood through the lens of ‘posh’ masculinity and the consumption of commodities.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how ‘posh’ masculinity is produced and consumed in contemporary Britain.
the micro-sociology of upward mobility, the role of the mass-media and the ‘posh’ masculinity which the mass-media has produced.
the micro-sociological processes that are involved in the qualitative, experential dimensions of upward mobility.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Changers’ experiences of upward mobility have been both liberating and constraining.

the Changers’ lives are characterised by an acute awareness that they have qualitatively changed their social position and that they are compelled to consume expensive commodities in an attempt to qualitatively replicate a ‘middleclass’ identity.
the Changers’ experiences and views reveal the complex, multifaceted, and paradoxical nature of social mobility.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the Changers’ social mobility is not a simple ‘upward’ movement but rather an ‘upward and outward’ journey, with the men having to negotiate the social and economic boundaries of their classed and gendered existences.

this study has revealed that upward mobility is a complex, multi-faceted process which is not only socially and culturally mediated by the mass-media but also has the potential to generate a range of anxieties and tensions within the upwardly mobile individual.
upward mobility is not simply a quantitative phenomenon, but also a highly qualitative, experientially complex one that is socially produced and experienced.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the Changers are not ‘middleclass’ and are not ‘middle-class’.
the Changers’ experiences and views are a microcosm of the broader phenomenon of upwardly mobile men in contemporary North-East Britain.
the qualitative dimensions of upward mobility should not be neglected in sociological research, especially when it comes to the lives of men.
